sentences.text: Aegirosaurus was an extinct genus of ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaurs belonging to the subfamily Platypterygiinae. The name translates to 'Aegir lizard with slender vertebrae', referencing the Norse sea god Aegir.

The neotype specimen measures 1.77 meters in length, while the destroyed holotype was estimated to be about 2 meters long. Aegirosaurus was a small ichthyosaur genus with adults measuring less than two meters in length.
The skull tapers into an elongate, thin snout that constitutes 62-73% of the lower jaw's length. The teeth of Aegirosaurus are firmly rooted in a groove within the jaw.
The eye sockets contain a scleral ring made of 14 bony plates that occupies most of the space within the orbit.
Aegirosaurus is estimated to have possessed approximately 157 vertebrae, including 52 presacral and 105 caudal vertebrae.
The tail of Aegirosaurus was bent downwards at an angle of roughly 45 degrees.

Aegirosaurus possessed six digits in each foreflipper, with five being primary digits that contacted the wrist. Each hindflipper of Aegirosaurus bears four digits, three of which are primary digits contacting the ankle.
Aegirosaurus possessed a tail fin shaped like a crescent moon.
Skin impressions on the neotype revealed wavy textures, straight fibrous tissue, and structures resembling very small scales.
The species was originally described by Wagner in 1853 as Ichthyosaurus leptospondylus. Aegirosaurus was originally described by Wagner in 1853.
Bardet and Fernández selected a neotype specimen in 2000 after the original holotype was destroyed in World War II.
Dental morphology and wear patterns suggest Aegirosaurus had a non-specialized diet.
Cladistic analyses place Aegirosaurus within the Platypterygiinae, which is the sister taxon to Ophthalmosaurinae.
Within the family Ophthalmosauridae, Aegirosaurus is most closely related to Ophthalmosaurus. Recent cladistic analyses suggest Aegirosaurus is more closely related to Sveltonectes.
The lineage of Aegirosaurus includes Brachypterygius and Maiaspondylus.
Aegirosaurus belongs to the subfamily Platypterygiinae. Aegirosaurus is classified in the family Ophthalmosauridae.
Fossils of Aegirosaurus have been found in the Lower Tithonian (Upper Jurassic) of Bavaria, Germany. Aegirosaurus fossils are known from the Tithonian (Late Jurassic) of Bavaria, Germany.

Aegirosaurus remains have also been discovered in the late Valanginian (early Cretaceous) of southeastern France. Aegirosaurus has recently been discovered in the late Valanginian (Early Cretaceous) of southeastern France.
Remains of Aegirosaurus were discovered in the limestone deposits of the Solnhofen Formation.
This French discovery represents the first diagnosed ichthyosaur from the Valanginian stage.
Aegirosaurus lived from 149.2 to 132.6 million years ago, spanning the Tithonian to Valanginian periods.
The presence of Aegirosaurus in both periods suggests that many late Jurassic ichthyosaurs survived across the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary.
It remains debated whether Aegirosaurus possessed scales, as microscopic confirmation is required to verify impressions resembling scales.
